name: The Alaska AI Docket
description: Every AI-infrastructure decision in Alaska. Land leases, comment windows, utility votes, legislation and federal solicitations, with the deciding body, the dates that matter, whether the public has a way in, and a fetched source for every fact.

fields.id: Stable kebab-case identifier. Never reused, never renamed.
fields.url: Canonical page for this decision on alaskaaihq.com.
fields.title: Plain-language headline for the decision.
fields.kind: What kind of decision this is. See enums.kind.
fields.status: Where the decision stands today. See enums.status.
fields.decider: The body that says yes or no.
fields.public_access: Whether the public has a formal way in RIGHT NOW. open means a comment or testimony path exists today, indirect means an elected or member-accountable body decides, closed means the evaluation is private.
fields.access_note: One or two sentences on how a member of the public reaches this.
fields.summary: One or two verified sentences describing the decision.
fields.key_dates: Dated milestones. Each carries a kind, which is its ROLE, and roles are not interchangeable. deadline is a date the READER must act by. vote is a body voting, often a different body than the decider. decision is the deciding body ruling. milestone is context. Only a deadline is ever a reader's call-to-action date.
fields.location: Place name with longitude and latitude in WGS84 degrees.
fields.sources: Every document a fact here was checked against, with the outlet and the date. Primary sources preferred. Nothing enters this dataset on rumour.
fields.first_seen: Date this decision entered the docket (America/Anchorage).
fields.last_updated: Date a human or the routine last re-verified it against a source.
fields.history: One dated line per material change, oldest first. This is the audit trail for how the decision moved.

items.title: STAK Energy's North Slope AI campus lease
items.decider: Alaska DNR, Division of Oil and Gas
items.access_note: The written comment window closed 4:30 p.m. July 17, 2026. DNR now weighs more than 500 comments before a final best-interest decision on the 50-year lease. No public comment path remains open.
items.summary: A preliminary decision would give STAK Energy a 50-year lease on 715.4 acres of state land about 26 miles south of Deadhorse for a gas-fired AI and cloud campus its developer pegs at more than $10 billion, with 1 to 3 gigawatts of on-site generation. More than 500 public comments arrived before the first deadline; fewer than a dozen supported the project.

items.title: Air Force land leases for AI data centers at JBER, Eielson and Clear
items.decider: Department of the Air Force, Enhanced Use Lease program
items.access_note: Proposals closed June 29 and are evaluated privately. No public comment period exists; no award timeline has been announced.
items.summary: The Air Force offered about 4,700 acres across 12 parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson AFB and Clear Space Force Station for privately financed AI data centers. Residents near the five Eielson-area parcels raised noise, permafrost and grid concerns, including one parcel less than a mile from North Pole Middle School.

key_dates.label: Program announced
Request for lease proposals released
Developer proposals due
Solicitation AFCEC-26-R-0006 archived with no award posted
U.S. House passes FY2027 NDAA carrying a data center lease restriction

Proposals due on a separate Eielson mixed-use lease covering 3,967 acres

history.note: Tracked. Bids closed June 29; no public word yet on how many proposals arrived.

Developer lease proposals closed June 29 and the Air Force is now in private evaluation of bids for up to 12 parcels across JBER, Eielson and Clear. The FY2027 NDAA reported by the Senate Armed Services Committee on June 23 would require a formal grid-impact assessment before the military can approve a data-center Enhanced Use Lease, a statutory check Interior utilities and ratepayers had sought.
Lease proposals were due June 29 and no developer selection or award has been made public as of this run. Carried forward as pending.

A July 19 industry analysis (AIX Energy) notes the Alaska Enhanced Use Lease solicitation for commercial AI data centers on about 4,700 acres across 12 parcels at JBER, Eielson and Clear has moved out of its open proposal phase with no developer award announced, and that unlike the Lower 48 portfolio (which set 100 MW and 500 million dollar minimums) the Alaska request's specific megawatt and capital thresholds are not disclosed. Carried forward as pending decision.

Re-verified by fetching the solicitation record for AFCEC-26-R-0006. The response deadline was June 29, 2026 at 5 p.m. EDT, extended from May 29, and the opportunity now reads Past Due with no award and no awardee recorded, last updated July 14, 2026. Twenty-six days past the deadline the three Alaska installations named in the request, JBER, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station, still have no publicly announced lessee. Evaluation is private, so there is no public comment room here.

Material update from Congress, verified against primary records. On July 22 at 4:37 p.m. the U.S. House passed H.R. 8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027, by 216 yea to 212 nay with 3 not voting, and Alaska Representative Nick Begich voted yea, per the House Clerk's roll call 278. Federal News Network reported that the House Armed Services chairman's mark carries an amendment from Rep. Cory Mills of Florida that bars the Defense Department from leasing its land to private companies to build data centers unless they agree not to install or operate data facility equipment containing components manufactured in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. Army officials warned the standard would drive world class commercial partners and more than 1.3 billion dollars in private capital away from Army land. If it survives conference it narrows who can bid on the Alaska parcels. The Senate has not passed its version. The underlying offer is unchanged, about 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station under the enhanced use lease model, which the Air Force says returns at least fair market value in cash.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act on July 23 with five cosponsors. It would permanently ban large AI data centers and associated infrastructure on land owned or managed by the United States, including military bases, and would require existing qualifying facilities to be removed and their sites remediated. The 4,700 acres offered here sit on exactly that kind of land. No award has been announced for the Alaska proposals, which were due June 29. Separately, the Air Force posted a second Eielson land solicitation on July 23 with an August 10 deadline, but that one is for mixed use development and is not part of this offering.

Re-checked the solicitation record for AFCEC-26-R-0006. It still reads Past Due with no award and no awardee, thirty-two days after the June 29 proposal deadline. The three Alaska installations named in the request still have no publicly announced lessee. Evaluation is private, so no public comment room exists here.

Re-verified today against the Air Force's own announcement, which states approximately 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station. That announcement sets no lease term in years, so the fifty year figure that has circulated elsewhere does not come from it. No developer selection has been made public as of this run.

A second and separate Eielson solicitation is now open. Request for Lease Proposal AFCEC-26-R-0009 covers four sites totalling 3,967 acres, held a virtual industry day on July 22, and takes proposals until August 10. The Air Force announcement describes it only as mixed-use development, listing residential, commercial, office, cultural, institutional and entertainment uses, and does not mention artificial intelligence or data centers. That is a description of the announcement. The lease document itself is posted on SAM.gov and has not been read here.

Still no selection announced. Lease proposals closed June 29, 2026 after an extension from May 29, and five weeks later there is no public award, shortlist or cancellation. Checked today against the Air Force announcement of the offer and the solicitation record for AFCEC-26-R-0006. The offer covers about 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at three installations on ground leases of up to fifty years, so a decision made quietly is a decision with a fifty-year tail.

Re-checked. The solicitation for AI data center development on the three installations closed to proposals on June 29 and was archived on July 14 with no award posted. The Air Force's own announcement describes approximately 4,700 acres across twelve parcels and quotes Deputy Assistant Secretary Robert Moriarty saying the offer supports the growing demands of the AI industry. Neither that announcement nor the solicitation record states how much electricity a project would draw.

The lease offer says the JBER sites do not have enough power. The Anchorage Daily News, reporting on the solicitation on May 5, 2026, quotes it describing those sites as having insufficient power for a data center and as requiring a new connection to Chugach Electric Association in Anchorage. Chugach's gas supply contract with Hilcorp Alaska, its primary supplier, ends in 2028.

No award and no developer selection has been announced, and the effort remains in solicitation.

The announcement says the opportunity will be awarded through a competitive source selection process, and it names no developer and no award. The record stands where it stood.

items.title: GVEA's $80 million turbine decision
items.decider: Golden Valley Electric Association board of directors
items.access_note: A member-owned co-op board decides, in executive session. GVEA members reach it through board elections and member comment periods at regular meetings.
items.summary: Golden Valley Electric Association is weighing a 60 megawatt naphtha fueled turbine estimated at $80 million, to be installed beside an existing LM6000 at the co-op's North Pole Expansion plant. Its board voted on August 25th, 2026 to keep the purchase alive and to keep studying the risks and the alternatives.

Board votes 4 to 3 in Delta Junction to move ahead on a possible purchase and to keep studying alternatives

history.note: Tracked ahead of the July 13 executive session.

Re-verified via KUAC and News-Miner ahead of the July 13 executive session. The Q3 fuel and purchased-power charge rose about 61 percent effective June 1, adding nearly $46 a month for an average residential member. Re-fetched the News-Miner report ahead of the July 13 special board meeting. The board weighs an LM6000 turbine costing about 120 million dollars, rated 45 to 58 MW alone and 76 to 152 MW if paired with steam or battery storage. In April the board approved 50,000 dollars to reserve an order spot plus a 25.6 million dollar overhaul of the 1970s GT1 diesel units. Some co-op members object to the added long-term debt.

The board was set to weigh the second LM6000 purchase in executive session on July 13, about 120 million dollars for a unit rated 45 to 58 MW alone and 76 to 152 MW paired with steam or storage. The News-Miner reports gas turbine demand has surged because large data centers need guaranteed power, while GVEA frames its own driver as higher load across the board. The vote outcome was not public as of this run, so status stays pending-decision. This is the anchor decision of Carousel No. 6.

A direct re-fetch of the GVEA newsroom returned HTTP 403 again and a search of Fairbanks reporting surfaced no public disclosure of the July 13 board decision on the second LM6000 purchase, consistent with a co-op board that deliberates in executive session. Five days after the July 13 special meeting a search of GVEA releases and Fairbanks reporting still surfaced no public disclosure of the board decision on the second LM6000 turbine, consistent with a co op board that deliberates in executive session. Status stays pending-decision and remains a hard re-check item.
Still no announced outcome from the July 13 board session. The cooperative's newsroom could not be reached today, so nothing here is changed.
Carried forward unchanged. The utility's newsroom could not be reached today and no report of a board decision on the turbine purchase was found.
Checked and unchanged. No board vote on the LM6000 purchase appears in Fairbanks reporting or in the utility's public filings, so the decision remains outstanding.
Re-verified. A special board meeting was scheduled for August 13th, and no decision on the roughly $120 million LM6000 purchase has surfaced in public reporting.

Checked and unchanged. No decision on the roughly $120 million LM6000 purchase has surfaced in public reporting since the special board meeting of August 13th, and KUAC's energy coverage still carries nothing on Golden Valley Electric Association later than the May 28th fuel charge story. The board's own site refuses an automated read, so the cooperative's decision, when it comes, will most likely be reported before it is posted.

The board acted. Meeting in Delta Junction on August 25th, 2026, the Golden Valley Electric Association board voted 4 to 3 on a motion by director Rick Solie to move ahead on a possible purchase, and agreed the same evening to keep studying the risks and the alternatives, wind among them. The unit is a 60 megawatt naphtha fueled turbine estimated at $80 million, and it would sit next to the older LM6000 at the North Pole Expansion plant. Board chair Dave Messier said the co-op wants to "make sure that we have turned over every stone and evaluated every alternative". This entry carried $120 million from earlier reporting on the same purchase, and $80 million is the figure the co-op's own board discussion now carries.

items.title: The AKLNG gas line tax bill
items.decider: Alaska Legislature, third special session
items.access_note: Legislators decide; constituents reach them directly. The gas line would feed the grid most Alaska compute would ride on.
items.summary: A conference committee compromise unveiled July 2 would swap the state property tax on the Glenfarne-led Alaska LNG project for a volumetric tax after five years of operation or 500 MMcf per day, and extend the completion deadline to the end of 2034. The House deadlocked 19 to 19 on July 16 over an expanded S corporation income tax, the governor rejected that provision, and a third special session convened July 27 with no bill from the governor and almost no legislators in the room.

Conferees unveiled a draft compromise on July 2 and set a floor vote for July 16, with the second special session ending July 19. Glenfarne owns 75 percent of the project. The sticking point is an S corporation corporate income tax provision that Governor Dunleavy has vowed to veto, and it is unclear the provision has the House votes. The draft also bars the developer from billing the state if the project is abandoned and requires return of shares and assets within six months.

Governor Dunleavy had asked lawmakers to return to Juneau on August 20th. The governor signalled the session is over. A tax break for the project now waits on a new governor and a new Legislature after the November election, which puts it in 2027 at the earliest.

items.title: Enstar's Cook Inlet gas storage plan (Kenai Loop Pool)
items.decider: Regulatory Commission of Alaska (prudency); Alaska DNR (storage lease and technical determination)

items.summary: On July 10, 2026 the Anchorage Daily News reported the RCA issued a 17-page order denying Enstar's request for an advance determination that its proposed Cook Inlet gas storage project was prudent, saying the utility lacked basic information. The $240 million project would have bought the depleted Kenai Loop Pool reservoir from AIX Energy to hold 25 billion cubic feet of gas, close to half Enstar's annual demand, adding up to $12 a month to the average bill. Enstar and Hilcorp have competing DNR lease applications for the same pool, and DNR has not confirmed it is technically capable of storing gas. Without approval, Enstar president John Sims said the company suspended the project. Enstar reopened the question on July 23, 2026 with a 31-page petition for reconsideration, arguing the order was erroneous and suffers from a lack of true understanding of the nature of the problem, and calling the Kenai Loop Pool the only viable commercial storage option in Cook Inlet. Alaska Public Media reports the commission has thirty days to respond and that inaction is an automatic denial.

items.summary: On March 27, 2026 the Anchorage Assembly adopted ordinance AO 2026-27 in a 10 to 2 vote, defining data centers in the municipal zoning code for the first time. items.summary: HB 259, introduced by Rep. Donna Mears in January 2026, would have set utility rate-setting guidelines and community benefit agreement standards for large energy use facilities such as data centers, and given the Regulatory Commission of Alaska new duties over them. The House Energy Committee heard it twice, on January 29th and February 3rd, 2026, taking testimony from Greensparc, GCI, the Alaska Municipal League and former Rep. Paul Seaton. It never advanced out of that committee, and it carried a second referral to House Community and Regional Affairs it never reached. The bill died with the 34th Legislature at sine die on May 20th, 2026. Alaska still has no statewide cost-allocation rule governing how a large data-center load is billed against other ratepayers, which leaves that question with the Regulatory Commission of Alaska and with individual utility boards.

items.title: The AI ratepayer pledge, and which Alaska utilities have signed it
items.decider: Each Alaska electric utility board, including the Railbelt cooperatives
items.access_note: Alaska's electric cooperatives are governed by boards their own members elect, so a member can ask their board directly whether it intends to sign. A voluntary federal pledge has no public comment docket, which is why this room is indirect rather than open.
items.summary: The White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge asks AI companies, utilities and data center developers to commit that new data center load pays for its own generation and delivery instead of shifting the cost onto households. USA TODAY and POWER both describe it as voluntary and non binding. Gov. Mike Dunleavy signed the governors addendum on July 23, 2026, one of 23 governors. Read live on July 26, 2026 the signatory list showed a single Alaska entity, Cordova Electric Cooperative, a 1,566 customer cooperative that is not connected by transmission line to any other community.

history.note: Tracked. The White House expanded the Ratepayer Protection Pledge on July 23 and 23 Republican governors signed an addendum committing to implement its principles to the greatest extent possible, Dunleavy among them. The pledge itself binds signing companies to five things, build bring or buy new power supply, pay for new delivery infrastructure, pay whether they use the power or not, invest in local jobs, and contribute to grid and community resilience. Both USA TODAY and POWER describe it as non binding. A read of the signatory list on July 26 returned one Alaska name, Cordova Electric Cooperative, and no Railbelt utility.

items.summary: The Alaska Energy Authority has asked FERC to amend the license for the Bradley Lake Hydroelectric Project, the largest in Alaska, so it can build a new dam diverting meltwater and surface runoff from the Dixon Glacier into Bradley Lake, raise the lake's normal maximum operating pool by about 16 feet, and install a 0.3 megawatt micro-hydro turbine in one of the dam's fishwater release valves. items.access_note: The state comment window closed at the end of the May 14th, 2026 hearing. The federal review of the application carries its own comment period, which has not opened.
items.summary: The Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission is applying to the Environmental Protection Agency for primary enforcement authority over Class VI wells, the wells used to inject carbon dioxide for permanent underground storage. If the application succeeds the state, not the federal government, would permit and police every carbon storage well in Alaska.

history.note: Tracked after a reader asked for the carbon capture approval process. The authority comes from two acts of the legislature, chapter 2 of the 2023 session laws directing the commission to seek this authority and chapter 23 of the 2024 session laws establishing the state carbon storage program. The commission held a public meeting on adopting its regulations on March 3rd, 2026 and a hearing on the application itself on May 14th, 2026, with comment closing at the end of that hearing. The commission has said it aims to complete the process in about two years, which other states' experience suggests is optimistic. This matters to the AI build out because the coal plant proposed in the Susitna watershed, tracked separately here, plans to inject its carbon dioxide into a depleted Cook Inlet gas reservoir, and these are the permits that would govern it.

items.title: The Kenai Peninsula school district's AI rulebook
items.decider: Kenai Peninsula Borough School District Board of Education
items.access_note: An elected school board decides, and its regular meetings carry a public comment period. There is no formal comment window on these documents and no published date for a final vote, so an Alaskan reaches this one through a board member or from the podium at a meeting.
items.summary: The Kenai Peninsula Borough School District is writing the rules for artificial intelligence in its 39 schools while the school year starts. Its Policy Review Committee took up AR 5131.9 Academic Honesty, a new administrative regulation the district says was brought forward in relation to the inclusion of AI, on August 3, 2026, with two competing drafts posted, one from Administration and one from board member Mica VanBuskirk. That same evening the full board took first readings on three more documents the district describes as revised for AI-related policy shifts, AR 5125 Student Records, BP 1114 Communication Using Electronic Media and BP 5131.9 Academic Honesty, plus AR 6161.4 Acceptable Use. Nothing in the package is adopted. The district told KBBI in July that it has spent 8,300 dollars to date on a three year MagicSchool subscription for students and staff, so the classroom AI tool was bought before the rulebook was finished. Upstream sits Alaska's Strategic Framework, Artificial Intelligence for K-12, issued by the Department of Education and Early Development, which means what Kenai adopts previews what other Alaska districts face.

items.title: DeepGreen's underwater data center in Cook Inlet
items.decider: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
items.access_note: There is no way to comment on this yet, and that is the whole state of it. FERC's spokesperson says the commission will request comments from the public after staff determine the application is complete, and a Federal Register search for DeepGreen on August 21st, 2026 returns nothing, so that step has not happened. The Federal Register is where the notice will appear when it does. The City of Kenai was told late, because FERC found the company had not notified it, and the Kenai city manager raised the proposal with councilors at their August meeting.
items.summary: DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV LLC, a Delaware company whose parent formed in January 2026, applied to FERC in February for a preliminary permit over an initial operational envelope of 1,650 acres of Cook Inlet seabed west of Nikiski, proposing a 100 megawatt data center of 66 hives of AI servers powered and cooled by approximately 330 to 350 tidal turbines in water 45 to 166 feet deep. A preliminary permit authorizes study rather than construction, for up to four years, and FERC's Northwest branch found the application incomplete in a June 18th letter.

key_dates.label: FERC's Northwest branch finds the application incomplete
First Alaska reporting on the filing

sources.outlet: Federal Register, Office of the Federal Register

history.note: Tracked from today. The applicant told FERC the project would tie into the Alaska Energy Authority's Cook Inlet PowerLink, a 38 mile subsea cable rated for up to 200 megawatts of bidirectional transfer that AEA lists as In Development and not yet built. AEA chief executive Curtis Thayer says the authority had never heard of DeepGreen and was never contacted, and that the company's letter to FERC has some of the project's facts "dead wrong". FERC also found the company had not identified all tribes and Alaska Native corporations that may be affected. The same company's Maine project at Eastport has been cut from 51 megawatts to a maximum of 15 and from about 170 turbines to 16 in a first phase, and Eastport's council voted unanimously on August 12th for a 180 day moratorium on any data center approval. The Maine Monitor reports the Alaska proposal has not been indicated as scaled down.

Checked the Federal Register for anything filed under this company. It carries exactly one DeepGreen notice, published August 25th, 2026, and that notice is for the Western Passage project in the Bay of Fundy near Eastport, Maine. It is not the Cook Inlet application. So the commission has now noticed the company's Maine filing and has not noticed the Alaska one.

The same developer's Maine application advanced and the Cook Inlet proposal did not. FERC accepted DeepGreen Western Passage SPV LLC's preliminary permit application for project P-15424-000, in the Western Passage of the Bay of Fundy near Eastport, Maine, and published the notice on August 25th, 2026. Comments, motions to intervene and competing applications on that project are due by 5:00 p.m. Eastern on October 19th, 2026. That notice does not mention Alaska or Cook Inlet, and no equivalent notice has published for the Cook Inlet proposal, whose last recorded federal action remains the June 18th, 2026 finding that the filing was incomplete.

items.title: Anchorage's surveillance rules for its police crime center
items.decider: Anchorage Assembly
items.access_note: The public hearing was set for the Assembly's September 1st meeting, which is where a member of the public could speak to this before the Assembly acts, and that meeting has now been held. The ordinance text and its AO number were still not published anywhere reachable as of September 1st, so anyone following it is working from press accounts and from the sponsors' own descriptions rather than from the statutory language, and the ordinance's disposition is not yet on the record here.
items.summary: Three Anchorage Assembly members, Keith McCormick, Sydney Scout and Vice Chair Daniel Volland, introduced an ordinance on August 18th that would write surveillance rules into Anchorage code, among them a case number for every search of surveillance data, deletion of individuals' data after two weeks unless it is evidence in an active investigation, a warrant before footage goes to out of state or federal agencies, limits on automatic license plate readers, and, in co-sponsor Scout's own words, Assembly approval before adding new surveillance capabilities including AI powered tracking or identification technology. It moves alongside a roughly $600,000 contract with ThunderCat Technology for equipment at the Real Time Crime Center, the system the Assembly funded with $11.8 million last year and which is designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds. The center opened in September 2025 with one employee and about 15 cameras.

history.note: Tracked, and selected as this run's carousel. The ordinance would put four rules in code before the camera network they govern is finished being built. What exists today is smaller than what is funded. The Assembly approved $11.8 million last year for a system designed to stream up to 750 camera feeds, and the center opened in September 2025 with one employee and about 15 cameras at police properties and Town Square Park. Police Chief Sean Case says the department uses object recognition for license plate readers, does not use facial recognition, and does not know whether object recognition data can even be transmitted through the system, so this is a rule arriving ahead of the capability rather than after it. One caution belongs on the record. Three published accounts word the AI provision three different ways and the ordinance text was not reachable, so the wording used here is the co-sponsor's own from her signed opinion piece.

Checked and unchanged. The public hearing is still set for September 1st, 2026, six days out. The ordinance by Keith McCormick, Sydney Scout and Daniel Volland would delete camera footage after two weeks unless it is part of an active investigation, hold license plate readers to traffic enforcement and justified tracking such as a missing child or a stolen vehicle, require a warrant before data goes to a federal agency, and require Assembly approval before the crime center uses artificial intelligence. The $600,000 ThunderCat contract behind it would reach roughly 750 cameras, including more than 250 traffic cameras alongside officer worn, private security and drone mounted feeds. McCormick said that when his constituents ask what is collected, who can see it and how long it is kept, Anchorage code can't answer those questions.

Checked against Alaska Public Media's August 21st report. The ordinance from Keith McCormick, Daniel Volland and Sydney Scout goes to public hearing on September 1st, 2026, the same meeting at which the Assembly takes up the roughly $600,000 ThunderCat contract for equipment at the crime center on Elmore Road. Staff would connect to about 750 cameras, including more than 250 city traffic cameras. Five days remain and nothing moved.

items.title: The FCC asks whether AI should help run the Universal Service Fund
items.decider: Federal Communications Commission
items.access_note: Anyone may file. Comments are due on or before September 30th, 2026 and reply comments on or before October 30th, 2026, in WC Docket No. 26-173, through the Commission's electronic filing system under 47 CFR 1.415 and 1.419. The notice gives Alaska no separate deadline and no separate route, so an Alaska clinic, school district, library or carrier files on the same clock as everyone else.
items.summary: The FCC published a notice on August 31st, 2026 seeking comment on how the Universal Service Fund is administered, and nine of its sentences name artificial intelligence. It asks whether AI tools used to review applications, audits and appeal review processes would reduce delays while maintaining accurate results, and whether the fund's administrator should expand use of AI in document review for audits and program compliance. One paragraph poses eight consecutive questions about AI. The Commission is asking rather than proposing, and every AI sentence in the notice is phrased as a question. The same notice seeks comment on cutting the administrator's board from 20 members to 13. Alaska is not named anywhere in it. Alaska's stake is in a companion notice published the same day, WC Docket No. 17-310, which reports that only 34 of 340 approved Telecom Program requests in Alaska in funding year 2025 relied on the Commission's preferred Methods 1 or 2, so the great majority of Alaska's rural health connectivity requests are justified the longer way. That is the paperwork an automated reviewer would read.
